researchStatement: Optimization and AI for coordinated, adaptive operations.
biography: I am a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus, working with Angela Kitali. My research integrates mathematical optimization and AI to study how operations and supply chain systems can coordinate decisions, adapt to disruption and use emerging technologies effectively.

I received my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering from Florida State University in August 2025, advised by Maxim A. Dulebenets, and continued there as a postdoctoral research scholar before joining Washington. I received my B.S. in Harbor, Waterway and Coastal Engineering from Wuhan University in June 2022.
homeResearch: My long-term research goal is to make optimization an adaptive part of how operations and supply chains are managed. This means studying the entire decision process: how operational knowledge becomes a mathematical model, how interdependent decisions are coordinated, and how plans are revised as conditions change. A central question is which decisions require joint optimization, and when coordination creates more value than additional capacity or flexibility.

My methodological work develops compact formulations, decomposition methods and algorithms that combine adaptive search with exact optimization. I use formulation structure to identify tractable subproblems and design how exact optimization and adaptive search interact. An emerging direction examines how learning and generative AI can extend this process, using domain knowledge to propose models or algorithms and computational feedback to evaluate and refine them.

The operational agenda spans coordination across organizations, resilience under disruption, and the joint planning of technology investment and operations. Information, incentives and decision authority shape which plans can be implemented; prior investment shapes the options available when conditions change. These questions motivate work across production and supply chains, as well as healthcare, humanitarian logistics and public services, where operational choices affect the continuity and accessibility of essential services.
academicContext: My training combines transportation engineering with operations research and computational optimization. After undergraduate study at Wuhan University, I pursued a Ph.D. at Florida State University, where my research focused on the mathematical and algorithmic structure of scheduling problems.

Working with Maxim A. Dulebenets, I developed hyperheuristic and hybrid optimization approaches for berth scheduling. Related studies extended to cross-docking, ship schedule recovery and infrastructure allocation. Together, these problems established my continuing interest in how modeling choices, adaptive computation and coordinated decisions affect operating performance.

I remained at Florida State University as a postdoctoral research scholar after completing my Ph.D. in August 2025. Since June 2026, I have worked with Angela Kitali at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus. My current transportation projects concern AI-assisted infrastructure inventories, while my broader research examines optimization, supply chain coordination and the design of adaptive operating systems.

My project experience includes research supported by the U.S. Department of Defense, Florida Department of Transportation and U.S. Department of Transportation. I am a co-principal investigator on the Washington speed-management inventory project. My educational work includes graduate instruction in optimization and freight facilities, undergraduate and master’s research mentorship, and external master’s thesis committee service.

homeQuestions: How can models and algorithms coordinate decisions across an entire operating system?
How should plans adapt to changing demand, limited capacity and disruption?
How can AI assist optimization while keeping decisions mathematically valid and interpretable?

collaborationProfiles.title: Mathematical optimization and logistics
collaborationProfiles.text: My doctoral and postdoctoral research with Maxim A. Dulebenets developed formulations and algorithms for berth scheduling and cross-docking. This collaboration examines how compact models, decomposition and adaptive search can exploit operational structure, with published studies addressing both the design of solution methods and their computational performance.
collaborationProfiles.label: Compact models and decomposition

collaborationProfiles.title: Transportation infrastructure and public decisions
collaborationProfiles.people: Angela Kitali and University of Washington collaborators
collaborationProfiles.text: My work with Angela Kitali concerns infrastructure information for transportation analysis. I contribute to the speed-management inventory as co-PI and to computer-vision methods for pedestrian and bicycle facilities. These studies examine the relationship between automated feature detection, spatial data quality and the planning questions an inventory can support.
collaborationProfiles.label: CTIL research team

collaborationProfiles.title: Safety and resource allocation
collaborationProfiles.people: Ren Moses, Eren E. Ozguven, John Sobanjo and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: Our highway-rail crossing research formulates closure selection as a resource-allocation problem with multiple consequences. The collaboration combines optimization with safety and infrastructure expertise to compare candidate choices and examine how input assumptions affect the resulting priorities.
collaborationProfiles.label: Rail-crossing decision study

collaborationProfiles.title: Adaptive algorithms and sustainable systems
collaborationProfiles.people: Marta Borowska-Stefańska, Szymon Wiśniewski, Yui-Yip Lau and research coauthors
collaborationProfiles.text: Joint publications address adaptive algorithms, maritime schedule recovery and sustainable supply chains. Across these studies, a shared interest is how computational methods represent interdependent decisions and expose trade-offs among operating objectives. Each publication provides the specific problem, contribution and complete author team.
